materialFindings.title: Fraud Detection Capability: Analytics, rules, reports or data checks are used to identify suspicious transactions, behaviour or control exceptions.

materialFindings.responseLabel: Consistently operating
materialFindings.responseOperationalMeaning: Operating consistently in practice.
materialFindings.responseMeaning: Consistently operating: Operating consistently in practice.
materialFindings.diagnosis: Analytics and rule-based detection was self-assessed as "Consistently operating" (Operating consistently in practice; normalised score 80/100). This is self-reported and requires the listed operating evidence before it can be treated as verified.
materialFindings.whyItMatters: This is an assurance priority, not a failed control. The strong self-reported response should be validated with operating evidence.
materialFindings.fraudMechanism: Manual review cannot cover transaction volume, so without data-driven tests the majority of activity is never examined and structured schemes persist undetected.
materialFindings.likelyFinancialImpact: Direct -- unreviewed exceptions can allow losses to compound.
materialFindings.likelyOperationalImpact: Alert backlogs can conceal important anomalies.
materialFindings.expectedControlStandard: A maintained catalogue of rules and data checks maps each test to a fraud scenario, runs against reconciled data, and is tuned from confirmed outcomes.

Source reconciliation evidence
Monthly tuning record with true/false positive outcomes

materialFindings.operatingFrequency: Scheduled rule execution at least monthly; monthly tuning review
minimumEvidenceCharacteristics: Each rule states scenario, source, threshold and reviewer
Results reconcile to source system totals
Tuning decisions are evidence-based

materialFindings.methodologyVersionId: MFRS-V1.2-CANDIDATE-OWNER-CORRECTION
materialFindings.responseLabel: Consistently operating
materialFindings.responseOperationalMeaning: Operating consistently in practice.
materialFindings.responseMeaning: Consistently operating: Operating consistently in practice.
materialFindings.diagnosis: Fraud awareness at induction was self-assessed as "Consistently operating" (Operating consistently in practice; normalised score 80/100). This is self-reported and requires the listed operating evidence before it can be treated as verified.
materialFindings.whyItMatters: This is an assurance priority, not a failed control. The strong self-reported response should be validated with operating evidence.
materialFindings.fraudMechanism: New joiners learn behaviour from whoever trains them, so without a formal baseline an existing workaround or bypass is transmitted as normal practice.
materialFindings.likelyFinancialImpact: Indirect -- staff may comply with fraudulent requests.
materialFindings.likelyOperationalImpact: Role-specific warning signs can be missed.
materialFindings.expectedControlStandard: Induction includes fraud content covering policy, reporting routes, consequences and role-relevant risks, is completed within a defined period of joining, and covers contractors where they hold equivalent access.

controls.controlObjective: Validate that "Fraud awareness is included in employee onboarding or induction" operates to its exact expected standard.
controls.targetState: Induction includes fraud content covering policy, reporting routes, consequences and role-relevant risks, is completed within a defined period of joining, and covers contractors where they hold equivalent access.
controls.controlDesign: Independently validate that "Fraud awareness is included in employee onboarding or induction" operates to the expected standard (Induction includes fraud content covering policy, reporting routes, consequences and role-relevant risks, is completed within a defined period of joining, and covers contractors where they hold equivalent access.) across the complete population, required frequency and under pressure. This does not assert a control defect; if validation identifies one, apply the recommended control design: The People lead must include a fraud module in induction covering the fraud policy and prohibited conduct, how and where to report, the protection from retaliation, the consequences of dishonest conduct, and the fraud risks specific to the joiner’s role; completion is required within a defined period of the start date, tracked against the joiner population from the HR system, extended to contractors with equivalent system or asset access, and overdue completion escalates to the hiring manager.

contradictions.whyItMatters: A control reported in place stops the scheme where an unauthorised payment leaves the bank only if the practices it relies on also operate.
contradictions.falseComfortRisk: Management may treat the scheme where an unauthorised payment leaves the bank as covered on the strength of one self-reported answer.
contradictions.whatLeadershipShouldVerify: Ask Financial controller or treasury manager to confirm how two authorisers for every payment works when capture and authorise separated is not in place.
contradictions.fraudPathwayEnabled: One person can release money, on the platform or through a branch instruction.

contradictions.title: Refunds approved independently is reported in place, but its supporting practices are not
contradictions.drivingResponses: Refunds approved independently: The system enforces the approval, and approvals are reviewed for patterns.; Refunds to the original source: Refunds are paid wherever the customer asks.
contradictions.whyItMatters: A control reported in place stops the scheme where refunds are stolen only if the practices it relies on also operate.
contradictions.falseComfortRisk: Management may treat the scheme where refunds are stolen as covered on the strength of one self-reported answer.
contradictions.whatLeadershipShouldVerify: Ask Customer service or finance manager to confirm how refunds approved independently works when refunds to the original source is not in place.
contradictions.fraudPathwayEnabled: One person raises and approves refunds or credit notes to themselves or accomplices.

contradictions.title: Daily reconciliation is reported in place, but its supporting practices are not
contradictions.drivingResponses: Daily reconciliation: Takings at every cash point are reconciled to sales records daily, and every shortage and surplus is investigated.; Dual control at hand-overs: Cash is counted at some handovers, such as at the end of the day, but not at shift changes.; Takings checked against an independent record: Partly: only in some areas, cases or periods; Deposits reconciled independently: Deposits are checked against the statement occasionally.
contradictions.whyItMatters: A control reported in place stops the scheme where cash takings are stolen only if the practices it relies on also operate.
contradictions.falseComfortRisk: Management may treat the scheme where cash takings are stolen as covered on the strength of one self-reported answer.
contradictions.whatLeadershipShouldVerify: Ask Store, branch or cash office manager to confirm how daily reconciliation works when dual control at hand-overs and takings checked against an independent record are not in place.
contradictions.fraudPathwayEnabled: Takings are under-recorded or removed before banking.

contradictions.title: Independent blind counts is reported in place, but its supporting practices are not
contradictions.drivingResponses: Independent blind counts: Every count is carried out or observed by people independent of the stores team, counting without sight of system quantities.; How stock is recorded: It is not formally recorded; Store access limited: No; Issues against approved requests: No
contradictions.whyItMatters: A control reported in place stops the scheme where stock is stolen and hidden in the counts only if the practices it relies on also operate.
contradictions.falseComfortRisk: Management may treat the scheme where stock is stolen and hidden in the counts as covered on the strength of one self-reported answer.
contradictions.whatLeadershipShouldVerify: Ask Financial controller to confirm how independent blind counts works when how stock is recorded and store access limited are not in place.
contradictions.fraudPathwayEnabled: The people who hold stock also count it.

contradictions.title: Multi-factor on all email is reported in place, but its supporting practices are not
contradictions.drivingResponses: Multi-factor on all email: Multi-factor authentication is required for every email account, including executives' and shared mailboxes, with no exceptions.; Mailbox rules and odd logins alerted: No
contradictions.whyItMatters: A control reported in place stops the scheme where an email account is taken over only if the practices it relies on also operate.
contradictions.falseComfortRisk: Management may treat the scheme where an email account is taken over as covered on the strength of one self-reported answer.
contradictions.whatLeadershipShouldVerify: Ask Head of IT or IT provider to confirm how multi-factor on all email works when mailbox rules and odd logins alerted is not in place.
contradictions.fraudPathwayEnabled: A mailbox without strong sign-in is used to send or intercept payment instructions.

contradictions.title: People know whom to tell is reported in place, but its supporting practices are not
contradictions.drivingResponses: People know whom to tell: All employees know at least two people they can tell, including one outside their reporting line, and that the Protected Disclosures Act protects them.; Speak-up channel: Only informally, such as telling a manager
contradictions.whyItMatters: A control reported in place stops the scheme where concerns are never reported only if the practices it relies on also operate.
contradictions.falseComfortRisk: Management may treat the scheme where concerns are never reported as covered on the strength of one self-reported answer.
contradictions.whatLeadershipShouldVerify: Ask HR manager or owner to confirm how people know whom to tell works when speak-up channel is not in place.
contradictions.fraudPathwayEnabled: People who suspect fraud have no safe route, or do not know whom to tell.

contradictions.title: Identities kept confidential is reported in place, but its supporting practices are not
contradictions.drivingResponses: Identities kept confidential: Reporters' identities are kept confidential, and access to reports is limited to a few named people.; Retaliation prohibited and punished: Allegations of retaliation are investigated and acted on, and the outcomes are reported to the board or owners.; Retaliation risk assessed: Partly: only in some areas, cases or periods

contradictions.falseComfortRisk: Management may treat the scheme where a reporter is exposed or retaliated against as covered on the strength of one self-reported answer.
contradictions.whatLeadershipShouldVerify: Ask Ethics officer or HR manager to confirm how identities kept confidential works when retaliation risk assessed is not in place.
contradictions.fraudPathwayEnabled: A reporter's identity leaks or they are penalised, and others stop reporting.

contradictions.title: Investigators independent is reported in place, but its supporting practices are not
contradictions.drivingResponses: Investigators independent: Every investigation is done by people independent of the area and the people being investigated, and conflicts are declared.; Who investigates: Line management or HR
contradictions.whyItMatters: A control reported in place stops the scheme where an investigation is not independent or fair only if the practices it relies on also operate.
contradictions.falseComfortRisk: Management may treat the scheme where an investigation is not independent or fair as covered on the strength of one self-reported answer.

contradictions.fraudPathwayEnabled: The investigator is too close to the matter, or conclusions ignore other explanations.

scenarios.title: No one is answerable for fraud risk

controlsExpected: Owner has authority across the organisation: the answer to "Does the person who handles fraud risk have the authority and budget to act across the organisation, not only in their own area?" is yes, across everything it should cover.
Dedicated fraud capability: the answer to "Is there a dedicated fraud risk or forensic function, or a defined external provider that fills that role?" is yes, across everything it should cover.
Annual fraud action plan: the answer to "Is there an annual plan or budget for fraud risk work?" is yes, across everything it should cover.

Qualified fraud leads: the answer to "Do the people who lead fraud risk work hold recognised training or qualifications, such as the CFE or forensic training?" is yes, across everything it should cover.
scenarios.concealmentMechanism: Executive accountable for fraud is reported in place, so management may not look further while owner has authority across the organisation and dedicated fraud capability are not.
scenarios.whyControlsMayNotCatchIt: Owner has authority across the organisation: not in place. Dedicated fraud capability: only in some areas, cases or periods. Annual fraud action plan: only in some areas, cases or periods.

Under-resourced or unqualified fraud capability
Management override of controls

leadershipDecisions.decisionRequired: Name one accountable executive for each area with first-priority schemes open or unsupported: risk assessment (2), procurement and third parties (2), people and payroll (2), cash, stock and assets (2), detection and response (2), governance (1), ethics and anti-corruption (1), finance and banking (1), customers and revenue (1) and digital and identity (1).
leadershipDecisions.evidenceDrivingIt: 0 first-priority schemes have a control that stops them reported as a gap, and 15 rely on a control whose own practices were reported as gaps.
leadershipDecisions.whyNow: Each scheme needs one person with authority over the process, the system and the people involved.
leadershipDecisions.recommendedDecision: Risk manager or fraud risk lead for risk assessment, Head of procurement or CFO for procurement and third parties, HR or payroll manager for people and payroll and Operations or financial manager for cash, stock and assets.
leadershipDecisions.implementationOwner: Risk manager or fraud risk lead
leadershipDecisions.oversightFunction: The board or its audit committee
leadershipDecisions.consequenceOfDelay: Schemes with no owner stay open, and the gaps that let them happen stay unassigned.
leadershipDecisions.immediateNextDeliverable: A signed list of schemes, their accountable executives and target dates.

leadershipDecisions.decisionRequired: Approve the target design for risk assessment, where 2 first-priority schemes are open or unsupported.
leadershipDecisions.evidenceDrivingIt: Fraud risks are never identified; AI-enabled schemes are not considered
leadershipDecisions.whyNow: The schemes share processes and owners; designing them together avoids separate partial fixes.
leadershipDecisions.recommendedDecision: Management formally accepts the results, and every significant risk has a named owner who has agreed to it. Process owners take part: the answer to "Do the people who run the processes take part, for example in workshops or interviews?" is yes, across everything it should cover. Processes walked through: the answer to "Does the assessment walk through each high-risk process step by step to find where fraud could happen?" is yes, across everything it should cover. Every risk is described as a specific scheme, with the perpetrator, the method and the process it affects.
leadershipDecisions.accountableExecutive: Risk manager or fraud risk lead
leadershipDecisions.implementationOwner: Risk manager or fraud risk lead
leadershipDecisions.oversightFunction: The board or its audit committee
leadershipDecisions.consequenceOfDelay: Controls are added one at a time and the scheme stays open through the gaps between them.
leadershipDecisions.immediateNextDeliverable: An approved control design with owners, operating cycle and the records each step leaves.

leadershipDecisions.decisionRequired: Put first the controls that other controls depend on.
leadershipDecisions.evidenceDrivingIt: Likelihood and impact rated is not in place, so harm beyond money, inherent and residual, common rating scale and compared with tolerance cannot operate; Written code of conduct is not in place, so code covers the key standards, code reaches everyone and annual acknowledgement cannot operate; Directors compared with staff is not in place, so how the staff comparison is done cannot operate.
leadershipDecisions.whyNow: Building the dependent checks first produces controls that cannot run.
leadershipDecisions.recommendedDecision: Sequence likelihood and impact rated, written code of conduct, directors compared with staff and dormant suppliers deactivated ahead of the checks that rely on them.
leadershipDecisions.accountableExecutive: Risk manager or fraud risk lead
leadershipDecisions.implementationOwner: Risk manager or fraud risk lead
leadershipDecisions.oversightFunction: The board or its audit committee
leadershipDecisions.consequenceOfDelay: Effort is spent on checks that cannot operate.

leadershipDecisions.decisionRequired: Decide whether to keep relying on 21 controls reported in place whose supporting practices were reported as gaps.
leadershipDecisions.evidenceDrivingIt: Executive accountable for fraud: 4 supporting practices reported as gaps; Fraud risks assessed: 4 supporting practices reported as gaps; AI-enabled fraud covered: 4 supporting practices reported as gaps.
leadershipDecisions.whyNow: A self-reported control that its own practices do not support can give management comfort it has not earned.
leadershipDecisions.recommendedDecision: Ask each process owner to confirm in writing how the control works without the missing practices, and close the practices in the next 60 days.
leadershipDecisions.oversightFunction: The board or its audit committee
leadershipDecisions.consequenceOfDelay: The scheme is treated as covered when it may not be.
leadershipDecisions.immediateNextDeliverable: Written confirmation from each process owner.

leadershipDecisions.decisionRequired: Have the board or its audit committee receive the status of the 15 first-priority schemes each month until they are closed.
leadershipDecisions.evidenceDrivingIt: 15 first-priority schemes open or unsupported across 10 areas.
leadershipDecisions.whyNow: Monthly reporting keeps the schemes visible to the people who can remove blockers.
leadershipDecisions.recommendedDecision: A one-page scheme status: owner, controls in place, controls outstanding, next date.
leadershipDecisions.implementationOwner: Risk manager or fraud risk lead
leadershipDecisions.oversightFunction: The board or its audit committee
leadershipDecisions.consequenceOfDelay: Progress is not visible until the next assessment.

cover.centralJudgement: Every first-priority fraud scheme is reported as covered, but 21 controls relied on are not supported in practice.

diagnosis.title: What is driving the position

rows.pattern: Executive accountable for fraud: reported in place, not supported by its practices

signals.title: Owner has authority across the organisation

rows.whyItMatters: It is relied on to stop the scheme where no one is answerable for fraud risk. One self-reported answer says it is in place; the answers about the practices it depends on say otherwise.

rows.pattern: Fraud risks assessed: reported in place, not supported by its practices
rows.whyItMatters: It is relied on to stop the scheme where fraud risks are never identified. One self-reported answer says it is in place; the answers about the practices it depends on say otherwise.

rows.pattern: AI-enabled fraud covered: reported in place, not supported by its practices
rows.whyItMatters: It is relied on to stop the scheme where AI-enabled schemes are not considered. One self-reported answer says it is in place; the answers about the practices it depends on say otherwise.

diagnosis.interpretation: Of 67 controls reported fully in place that the method can cross-check, 10 were cross-checked with one further self-reported answer about a practice they depend on: 0 consistent, 6 conflicting, 1 partial operation and 3 narrower scope. The other 57 were not cross-checked and nothing is concluded about them. These cross-checks compare the organisation's own answers; they are not tests of operation and they change no figure.

rows.exposure: A fictitious supplier is created and paid
rows.whyItMatters: Fictitious suppliers enter through onboarding that can be skipped.

assessmentBasis.title: New supplier approved by another person

rows.potentialConsequence: Funds paid to a diverted, fictitious or overbilling supplier, often unrecoverable once released.
rows.interruptionPoint: Directors and owners, including those behind holding companies, are identified for every new supplier from an independent source.
rows.priorityBasis: First-priority scheme; its control is reported in place, but 5 practices it relies on are gaps.

rows.exposure: Invoices are paid for goods or services not received or not agreed
rows.whyItMatters: Invoices paid without checking approval and receipt are how overbilling and fictitious deliveries get paid.
rows.potentialConsequence: Funds paid to a diverted, fictitious or overbilling supplier, often unrecoverable once released.
rows.interruptionPoint: Every purchase is approved by someone with the authority to do so before the organisation commits, and the approval is recorded.
rows.priorityBasis: First-priority scheme; its control is reported in place, but 3 practices it relies on are gaps.

rows.whyItMatters: Whether risks are understood decides whether controls are aimed at the right schemes.
rows.potentialConsequence: Losses grow because unusual activity is not seen or challenged in time.
rows.interruptionPoint: Management formally accepts the results, and every significant risk has a named owner who has agreed to it.
rows.priorityBasis: First-priority scheme; its control is reported in place, but 4 practices it relies on are gaps.

rows.whyItMatters: A payroll that nobody independent reviews before payment is where ghost employees hide.

assessmentBasis.title: New employee checked by another person

rows.potentialConsequence: Salaries paid to fictitious, departed or overpaid employees, recurring every pay run until found.
rows.interruptionPoint: Every new record is checked against a signed appointment by someone other than the person who captured it, before the first pay run.
rows.priorityBasis: First-priority scheme; its control is reported in place, but 3 practices it relies on are gaps.

scenarios.title: How the schemes would work here
A fictitious supplier is created and paid
scenarios.entryPoint: An insider or outsider adds a supplier that does not exist and invoices it.
scenarios.entryPointShort: An insider or outsider adds a supplier that does not exist and invoices it
scenarios.controlBreak: Every new supplier goes through a defined process, with set checks and an approval, before it can be paid. New supplier approved by another person: not in place. Directors compared with staff: not in place.
scenarios.controlBreakShort: New supplier process reported in place
scenarios.howItUnfolds: An insider or outsider adds a supplier that does not exist and invoices it. Fictitious suppliers enter through onboarding that can be skipped. Here, new supplier process is reported in place, but new supplier approved by another person: not in place; directors compared with staff: not in place.
warningIndicators: Fictitious or shell suppliers
Undisclosed conflicts of interest
Misrepresented supplier credentials
scenarios.immediateInterruption: Until the design operates, the process owner puts every new case and the recent ones to this test by hand: Does someone other than the person who captured a new supplier approve it before it becomes active?

scenarios.title: Invoices are paid for goods or services not received or not agreed
scenarios.entryPoint: Overbilling, fictitious deliveries or inflated rates are paid.
scenarios.entryPointShort: Overbilling, fictitious deliveries or inflated rates are paid
scenarios.controlBreak: Every invoice is checked against an approved order, quote or contract and against confirmation of receipt before payment, and differences are resolved first. Services confirmed: not in place. Most purchases are approved before commitment, through a purchase order or another record.
scenarios.controlBreakShort: Three-way match reported in place; services confirmed not in place
scenarios.howItUnfolds: Overbilling, fictitious deliveries or inflated rates are paid. Invoices paid without checking approval and receipt are how overbilling and fictitious deliveries get paid. Here, three-way match is reported in place, but services confirmed: not in place; most purchases are approved before commitment, through a purchase order or another record.
warningIndicators: Unauthorised commitments and approval override
Duplicate or false invoices
Overpricing, overbilling and inflated variations
scenarios.immediateInterruption: Until the design operates, the process owner puts every new case and the recent ones to this test by hand: For services, does the person receiving the service confirm it was delivered before payment?

scenarios.title: Fraud risks are never identified
scenarios.entryPoint: Management does not know how fraud could happen in its own processes.
scenarios.entryPointShort: Management does not know how fraud could happen in its own processes
scenarios.controlBreak: Fraud risks assessed: in place. Management has not seen or accepted the results. Process owners take part: not in place.
scenarios.controlBreakShort: Fraud risks assessed reported in place; management owns the results not in place
scenarios.exposureShort: Fraud schemes that are never identified, so no control is designed to stop them
scenarios.howItUnfolds: Management does not know how fraud could happen in its own processes. Whether risks are understood decides whether controls are aimed at the right schemes. Here, fraud risks assessed is reported in place, but management has not seen or accepted the results; process owners take part: not in place.
warningIndicators: Fraud schemes that are never identified, so no control is designed to stop them
Effort and audit work not directed at the highest fraud risks
Controls that do not match how fraud actually happens
scenarios.immediateInterruption: Until the design operates, the process owner checks every new case and the recent ones by hand against this standard: management formally accepts the results, and every significant risk has a named owner who has agreed to it.

actions.completionTest: Every first-priority scheme has a named executive and a date.

actions.action: Confirm with CEO or company secretary how executive accountable for fraud operates and put in place owner has authority across the organisation, dedicated fraud capability and annual fraud action plan.

actions.completionTest: Management's own records show, for every case in the period: management formally accepts the results, and every significant risk has a named owner who has agreed to it.

decisionAgenda.decisionRequired: Name one accountable executive for each area with first-priority schemes open or unsupported: risk assessment (2), procurement and third parties (2), people and payroll (2), cash, stock and assets (2), detection and response (2), governance (1), ethics and anti-corruption (1), finance and banking (1), customers and revenue (1) and digital and identity (1).
decisionAgenda.whyNow: Each scheme needs one person with authority over the process, the system and the people involved.
decisionAgenda.recommendedDirection: Risk manager or fraud risk lead for risk assessment, Head of procurement or CFO for procurement and third parties, HR or payroll manager for people and payroll and Operations or financial manager for cash, stock and assets.
decisionAgenda.consequenceOfDelay: Schemes with no owner stay open, and the gaps that let them happen stay unassigned.

decisionAgenda.decisionRequired: Approve the target design for risk assessment, where 2 first-priority schemes are open or unsupported.
decisionAgenda.whyNow: The schemes share processes and owners; designing them together avoids separate partial fixes.
decisionAgenda.recommendedDirection: Management formally accepts the results, and every significant risk has a named owner who has agreed to it. Process owners take part: the answer to "Do the people who run the processes take part, for example in workshops or interviews?" is yes, across everything it should cover. Processes walked through: the answer to "Does the assessment walk through each high-risk process step by step to find where fraud could happen?" is yes, across everything it should cover. Every risk is described as a specific scheme, with the perpetrator, the method and the process it affects.
decisionAgenda.consequenceOfDelay: Controls are added one at a time and the scheme stays open through the gaps between them.

decisionAgenda.decisionRequired: Put first the controls that other controls depend on.
decisionAgenda.whyNow: Building the dependent checks first produces controls that cannot run.
decisionAgenda.recommendedDirection: Sequence likelihood and impact rated, written code of conduct, directors compared with staff and dormant suppliers deactivated ahead of the checks that rely on them.
decisionAgenda.consequenceOfDelay: Effort is spent on checks that cannot operate.

decisionAgenda.decisionRequired: Decide whether to keep relying on 21 controls reported in place whose supporting practices were reported as gaps.
decisionAgenda.whyNow: A self-reported control that its own practices do not support can give management comfort it has not earned.
decisionAgenda.recommendedDirection: Ask each process owner to confirm in writing how the control works without the missing practices, and close the practices in the next 60 days.
decisionAgenda.consequenceOfDelay: The scheme is treated as covered when it may not be.

decisionAgenda.decisionRequired: Have the board or its audit committee receive the status of the 15 first-priority schemes each month until they are closed.
decisionAgenda.whyNow: Monthly reporting keeps the schemes visible to the people who can remove blockers.
decisionAgenda.recommendedDirection: A one-page scheme status: owner, controls in place, controls outstanding, next date.
decisionAgenda.consequenceOfDelay: Progress is not visible until the next assessment.

findings.assessedPosition: Every new supplier goes through a defined process, with set checks and an approval, before it can be paid.
findings.assessedDiagnosis: new supplier process was reported in place, but 5 practices that it relies on were reported as gaps. New supplier approved by another person: not in place. Directors compared with staff: not in place. Dormant suppliers deactivated: not in place. Suppliers re-checked: set out but not yet working in practice. The confirmation may therefore give more comfort than the practice supports. Reported by the respondent and Procurement; not independently tested.
findings.fraudMechanism: An insider or outsider adds a supplier that does not exist and invoices it. The method links it to fictitious or shell suppliers, undisclosed conflicts of interest, misrepresented supplier credentials and duplicate or false invoices.
findings.whyItMatters: Fictitious suppliers enter through onboarding that can be skipped.

findings.assessedPosition: Every invoice is checked against an approved order, quote or contract and against confirmation of receipt before payment, and differences are resolved first.
findings.assessedDiagnosis: three-way match was reported in place, but 3 practices that it relies on were reported as gaps. Services confirmed: not in place. Most purchases are approved before commitment, through a purchase order or another record. Receipt is recorded for most deliveries, but not always before payment. The confirmation may therefore give more comfort than the practice supports. Reported by Procurement, Operations and sales and the respondent; not independently tested.
findings.fraudMechanism: Overbilling, fictitious deliveries or inflated rates are paid. The method links it to unauthorised commitments and approval override, duplicate or false invoices, overpricing, overbilling and inflated variations, goods or services paid for but not received, counterfeit, substituted or substandard goods and misrepresented supplier credentials.
findings.whyItMatters: Invoices paid without checking approval and receipt are how overbilling and fictitious deliveries get paid.

findings.assessedPosition: Yes, in a dedicated fraud risk assessment
findings.assessedDiagnosis: fraud risks assessed was reported in place, but 4 practices that it relies on were reported as gaps. Management has not seen or accepted the results. Process owners take part: not in place. Processes walked through: not in place. Some risks describe a scheme, but most remain general. The confirmation may therefore give more comfort than the practice supports. Reported by the respondent and Risk and investigations; not independently tested.
findings.fraudMechanism: Management does not know how fraud could happen in its own processes. The method links it to fraud schemes that are never identified, so no control is designed to stop them, effort and audit work not directed at the highest fraud risks, controls that do not match how fraud actually happens, blind spots in parts of the organisation or in types of fraud, an assessment that falls out of date as the business and threats change, management override of controls not considered, unable to show regulators, courts or funders that fraud risk was managed, fraud committed for the organisation's benefit goes unrecognised and AI-enabled fraud not anticipated.
findings.whyItMatters: Whether risks are understood decides whether controls are aimed at the right schemes.

findings.assessedPosition: Yes, across everything it should cover
findings.assessedDiagnosis: code accessible to staff was reported in place, but 4 practices that it relies on were reported as gaps. Written code of conduct: not in place. Programme independently reviewed: not in place. Trends reported upward: not in place. Training on joining: set out but not yet working in practice. scenarios.title: A fictitious supplier is created and paid
scenarios.actorClass: An insider or outsider relying on a control that is reported but not supported
scenarios.opportunity: New supplier approved by another person: not in place. Directors compared with staff: not in place. Dormant suppliers deactivated: not in place.
scenarios.entryPoint: An insider or outsider adds a supplier that does not exist and invoices it.
scenarios.mechanism: Fictitious suppliers enter through onboarding that can be skipped. What the answers show: New supplier approved by another person: not in place. Directors compared with staff: not in place. Dormant suppliers deactivated: not in place.
scenarios.concealment: New supplier process is reported in place, so management may not look further while new supplier approved by another person and directors compared with staff are not.
scenarios.consequence: Funds paid to a diverted, fictitious or overbilling supplier, often unrecoverable once released. Supplier relationships, payment runs and the supplier master file would need to be investigated and corrected.
warningIndicators: Fictitious or shell suppliers
Undisclosed conflicts of interest
Misrepresented supplier credentials
Duplicate or false invoices
scenarios.controlWeakness: New supplier approved by another person: not in place; Directors compared with staff: not in place; Dormant suppliers deactivated: not in place; Suppliers re-checked: set out but not yet working in practice; Directors identified: only in some areas, cases or periods
scenarios.interruptionPoint: New supplier approved by another person: the answer to "Does someone other than the person who captured a new supplier approve it before it becomes active?" is yes, across everything it should cover. Directors compared with staff: the answer to "Do you compare supplier directors, owners, addresses or bank accounts with your employee records?" is yes, across everything it should cover. Dormant suppliers deactivated: the answer to "Are suppliers that have not been used for a set period deactivated?" is yes, across everything it should cover. Suppliers re-checked: the answer to "Are existing suppliers re-checked periodically, not only when they are first added?" is yes, across everything it should cover. Directors and owners, including those behind holding companies, are identified for every new supplier from an independent source.
scenarios.immediateContainment: Until the design operates, the process owner puts every new case and the recent ones to this test by hand: Does someone other than the person who captured a new supplier approve it before it becomes active?
scenarios.longTermResponse: New supplier approved by another person: the answer to "Does someone other than the person who captured a new supplier approve it before it becomes active?" is yes, across everything it should cover. Directors compared with staff: the answer to "Do you compare supplier directors, owners, addresses or bank accounts with your employee records?" is yes, across everything it should cover. Dormant suppliers deactivated: the answer to "Are suppliers that have not been used for a set period deactivated?" is yes, across everything it should cover.

scenarios.title: Invoices are paid for goods or services not received or not agreed
scenarios.actorClass: An insider or outsider relying on a control that is reported but not supported
scenarios.opportunity: Services confirmed: not in place. Most purchases are approved before commitment, through a purchase order or another record. Receipt is recorded for most deliveries, but not always before payment.
scenarios.entryPoint: Overbilling, fictitious deliveries or inflated rates are paid.
scenarios.mechanism: Invoices paid without checking approval and receipt are how overbilling and fictitious deliveries get paid. What the answers show: Services confirmed: not in place. Most purchases are approved before commitment, through a purchase order or another record. Receipt is recorded for most deliveries, but not always before payment.
scenarios.concealment: Three-way match is reported in place, so management may not look further while services confirmed and approved order before commitment are not.
scenarios.consequence: Funds paid to a diverted, fictitious or overbilling supplier, often unrecoverable once released. Supplier relationships, payment runs and the supplier master file would need to be investigated and corrected.
warningIndicators: Unauthorised commitments and approval override
Duplicate or false invoices
Overpricing, overbilling and inflated variations
Goods or services paid for but not received
Counterfeit, substituted or substandard goods
Misrepresented supplier credentials
scenarios.controlWeakness: Services confirmed: not in place; Approved order before commitment: only in some areas, cases or periods; Receipt recorded before payment: only in some areas, cases or periods
scenarios.interruptionPoint: Services confirmed: the answer to "For services, does the person receiving the service confirm it was delivered before payment?" is yes, across everything it should cover. Every purchase is approved by someone with the authority to do so before the organisation commits, and the approval is recorded. Receipt is always recorded before the related invoice is paid.
scenarios.immediateContainment: Until the design operates, the process owner puts every new case and the recent ones to this test by hand: For services, does the person receiving the service confirm it was delivered before payment?
scenarios.longTermResponse: Services confirmed: the answer to "For services, does the person receiving the service confirm it was delivered before payment?" is yes, across everything it should cover. The system prevents commitment without approval, and purchases made without one are reported and followed up. The system will not pay without a receipt record, and gaps are reported.

scenarios.entryPoint: Management does not know how fraud could happen in its own processes.

Blind spots in parts of the organisation or in types of fraud

scenarios.mechanism: Daily reconciliation of takings is the main control over cash theft. What the answers show: Cash is counted at some handovers, such as at the end of the day, but not at shift changes. Takings checked against an independent record: only in some areas, cases or periods. Deposits are checked against the statement occasionally.
scenarios.concealment: Daily reconciliation is reported in place, so management may not look further while dual control at hand-overs and takings checked against an independent record are not.
scenarios.consequence: Cash taken before or after it is recorded, typically in small amounts over a long period. Cash records, banking and till reconciliations would need to be rebuilt for the affected period.
warningIndicators: Theft of cash
Sales skimmed before they are recorded
Fake proof of payment, deposit or delivery
scenarios.controlWeakness: Dual control at hand-overs: only in some areas, cases or periods; Takings checked against an independent record: only in some areas, cases or periods; Deposits reconciled independently: only in some areas, cases or periods

scenarios.immediateContainment: Until the design operates, the process owner checks every new case and the recent ones by hand against this standard: whenever cash changes hands, two people count it, record it and sign for it.
scenarios.longTermResponse: Count records are reviewed against takings, and any handover without two signatures is followed up. Delays and differences are investigated, and a deposit slip is never accepted as proof without the bank record.
